Chiapas, Mexico

Where San Cristóbal de las Casas gets its water, and where the water goes

The city pumps its water from springs on the floor of a closed mountain valley and returns it, untreated, to the rivers. This page follows the water through seven stages, from rain to the fields below the city.

How the city’s water sources compare
Notes on the data
  1. Rainfall. The valley has one long-running rain gauge, La Cabaña, on the valley floor (1,153 mm a year, 1991–2020). The map shading is an estimate: the gauge figure is raised by 110 mm for every 100 m of height, a rate chosen so that the hills average the 1,405 mm implied by a 2011 runoff study. On that basis the basin receives between 330 and 402 million m³ a year.
  2. Where the rain goes. Runoff is from a 2011 study and evaporation is calculated from climate data. The amount that soaks into the ground is what remains, so it is the least certain: with the higher rainfall estimate in note 1 it could be as much as 106 million m³.
  3. Wells and chlorination. No source explains the depth of SAPAM’s wells. The 2012–13 samples were taken at tanks and pump sumps, where chlorine is added; the study reports that doses were often too low and that not every source was treated every day, and it did not trace where the bacteria came from. The count of five chlorination points before 2020 is SAPAM’s own. Chlorine does not reliably kill some parasites, such as Cryptosporidium.
  4. Leaks and delivery. Pipe losses have not been measured. Published reports assume 30% to 50%; this page uses 40%, which gives 80 to 105 litres per person per day across that range. The split of delivered water also assumes 10% is consumed. SAPAM has not published an explanation for the rationing; the causes listed are those recorded in its own reports and in the press.
  5. People, quality and days of supply by source. People served is each source’s share of SAPAM customers in 2011, applied to the 212,700 people SAPAM said it supplied in 2019, rounded to the nearest thousand. Bacteria results are from sampling at each source in 2012–13, and days of supply from utility records for 2012–14. Neither has been published for later years, so the cards give these as the latest figures. Neighbourhoods are matched to sources from SAPAM’s published list; Outlines on the state plan that the list does not name are shown in light grey as unknown source.
  6. Water used per person, and water from outside the pipes. The bars are not strictly like for like. San Cristóbal (2020) is this page’s estimate of water reaching all users, businesses included. Oaxaca state (2020) is the 107 litres supplied per person recorded by the national environmental information system, less the 20% to 30% the Oaxaca city utility estimates is lost to leaks. Turkey (2022) is water supplied to households, from state statistics, divided by a population of 85 million. England (2025–26) is measured household use, from the Environment Agency. The 50 to 100 litres is the range the World Health Organization and the United Nations give for a person’s basic needs. Bottled water: a 2017 market survey found that Mexican households bought 1,385 litres a year, about one litre a person a day; no figure exists for San Cristóbal. Tanker and unpiped homes are from the 2020 census. The Coca-Cola plant’s licence volume is as registered with CONAGUA.
  7. River pollution. The four classes follow the scale used by CONAGUA, the federal water commission, for biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), the oxygen that bacteria use up breaking down the waste in a litre of water. “Clean” is its excellent and good classes (up to 6 mg/L), “slightly polluted” its acceptable class (6 to 30), “polluted” its contaminated class (30 to 120) and “heavily polluted” its heavily contaminated class (over 120). The count of more than 4,000 pipes is from a 2018 study by Sulca and Fonseca and probably includes individual household connections; CONAGUA inspected five outlets in 2014, and the National Human Rights Commission saw at least 14 in 2020. The scale measures organic waste, not faecal bacteria. CONAGUA’s monitoring classes the Río Amarillo as contaminated with faecal bacteria (1,000 to 10,000 per 100 mL) where it enters the city; the World Health Organization’s guideline for watering crops eaten raw is 1,000. Each point’s class is taken as the median of the state’s tests at each sampling point in 2022–23 (wetlands 2022). River widths on the map show streams, rivers and the joined river; they are not scaled to measured flow. The 5.3 million m³ of sewage is the delivered water less the share assumed to be consumed. A separate estimate, which multiplies the whole population by 114 to 160 litres a day, gives 9 to 13 million m³; sewers also take in rain and groundwater.
  8. Tunnel flow and floods. Nothing has been measured at the tunnel. The lower figure, 124 million m³ a year, is the mean annual runoff of the basin given in the wetland-treaty documents; the upper, 196, is the result of an uncalibrated computer model. The sewage share uses this page’s 5.3 million m³. No estimate has been published of the chance of the tunnel failing or of how often a storm exceeds its capacity; one press report, citing unnamed experts, puts the limit at about 95 mm of rain in an hour. The account of the sinkholes, the 1973 flood and the spread of the city onto the low ground is from Montoya and others (2008), who link the blocked sinkholes to the rapid occupation of the valley but give no period; the president’s order is from a local history. Flood counts are from SAPAM (2020) and the state fire service as reported in the press (2022).
  9. Below the tunnel. The families, villages, area and crops are from one press report of 2020, which cites a farm-technology institute; other sources count 21 or 32 communities. No map of the plots has been published, so the fields are not drawn. The World Health Organization guidance is its 2006 guideline on wastewater in agriculture; the Mexican limit is from the federal discharge standard in force since 2023. No published test of the crops or soil, record of precautions taken by farmers or sellers, or measurement further downstream was found. The underground route to San Lucas has not been confirmed by tracing.
  10. How things are placed on the map. Streets, waterways, ponds and marshes are from OpenStreetMap. Contours, neighbourhood outlines, census coverage by block and public buildings are from the Chiapas state infrastructure plan of 2022; block outlines were traced from its inset maps and can be a few tens of metres out. The protected-area boundary is the official one. Relief outside the city, the flood-prone ground and the rainfall shading use satellite heights accurate to a few metres. Symbols with a dashed outline were placed from written descriptions and can be several hundred metres out. Pipes are drawn as straight lines between known ends, because their routes have not been published. Main sewers are not drawn at all: only the five points where they empty into the Río Amarillo have published coordinates, from a federal inspection in 2014.
